reason: The sources contain highly detailed, overlapping accounts of the siege, providing 20 robust claims supported by multiple independent sites with exact quotes.
story: In May 1565, a massive Ottoman armada carrying up to 40,000 soldiers descended on the rocky island of Malta, determined to wipe the 500 Knights of St. John off the earth. Led by the seventy-year-old Grand Master Jean de Valette, the defenders poisoned their own wells, harvested unripened crops, and prepared for total war. The Ottomans first targeted Fort St. Elmo, expecting a quick victory, but the small garrison held out for a month, costing the invaders thousands of lives and their famous admiral, Dragut. When the fort finally fell, the Ottomans floated decapitated knights on mock crucifixes across the harbor. In ruthless retaliation, Valette beheaded his Turkish prisoners and fired their heads back from cannons. Against impossible odds, Senglea and Birgu held through months of horrific bombardment until a Sicilian relief fleet finally arrived in September, forcing the shattered Ottoman army to retreat.
angle: To shatter enemy morale after capturing Fort St. Elmo, the Ottomans floated the decapitated bodies of knights on mock crucifixes across the harbor; in ruthless retaliation, Grand Master Jean de Valette beheaded his Turkish prisoners and fired their heads from his cannons into the enemy camp.

claims.claim: The Great Siege of Malta took place in 1565 when the Ottoman Empire attempted to conquer the island from the Knights Hospitaller.

evidence.quote: occurred in 1565 when the Ottoman Empire attempted to conquer the island of Malta, then held by the Knights Hospitaller.
took place in 1565, when the Ottoman Empire invaded the island, then held by the Knights Hospitaller

claims.claim: The defenders held out against the siege for nearly four months.

evidence.quote: The siege lasted nearly four months
They held out for nearly four months

claims.claim: In 1530, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V granted Malta to the Knights.

evidence.quote: granted to them by Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor in return for one falcon sent annually
granted to them by Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.

claims.claim: In 1522, Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent had forced the Knights out of Rhodes after a six-month siege.

evidence.quote: Suleiman the Magnificent, the Ottoman Sultan, had forcibly ejected the Knights from their base on Rhodes after the six-month siege of Rhodes.
the Knights had been forced from their base on Rhodes by the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent after a siege of six months' duration.

claims.claim: In preparation for the siege, Grand Master Jean Parisot de Valette raised troops in Italy, laid in stores, and repaired key forts.

evidence.quote: De Valette set about raising troops in Italy, laying in stores and finishing work on Fort Saint Angelo, Fort Saint Michael, and Fort Saint Elmo.
Valette set about raising troops in Italy, laying in stores and finishing repairs on Fort Saint Angelo, Fort Saint Michael, and Fort Saint Elmo.

claims.claim: Before the Turkish invaders arrived, de Valette had all crops harvested and poisoned the wells with bitter herbs and dead animals.

evidence.quote: de Valette ordered the harvesting of all the crops, including unripened grain, to deprive the enemy of any local food supplies. Furthermore, the Knights poisoned all wells with bitter herbs and dead animals.
ordered that all the crops be harvested, including unripened grain, thus depriving the Turks of any local food supplies. Furthermore all the wells were poisoned, with bitter herbs and dead animals.

claims.claim: The Ottoman force sent to invade Malta was estimated to be around 40,000 fighting men.

evidence.quote: estimate we could make of the enemy's force was 40,000 fighting men.
carrying an army estimated to be 40,000 strong

claims.claim: A disagreement arose within the Ottoman command, with Mustafa Pasha intending to attack the inland capital of Mdina first.

evidence.quote: Mustafa intended, according to these accounts, to attack the poorly defended former capital Mdina, which stood in the centre of the island
Mustafa wanted to capture Mdina and move onto the coastal forts

claims.claim: The famous Ottoman admiral and privateer Dragut was killed during the siege.

evidence.quote: hit Dragut in the head, killing him
Dragut was killed during this phase, struck by stone splinters

claims.claim: Fort St. Elmo fell to the Ottomans on June 23.

evidence.quote: Finally, on 23 June, the Turks seized what was left of Fort St. Elmo.
By the time St Elmo fell on 23 June

claims.claim: The siege of Fort St. Elmo cost the Ottoman invaders an estimated 6,000 casualties.

evidence.quote: the siege of Fort St. Elmo had cost the Turks at least 6,000 men
the Ottomans had lost an estimated 6,000 men

claims.claim: The Ottomans decapitated the dead knights and floated their bodies across the bay on mock crucifixes.

evidence.quote: Mustafa had the bodies of the knights decapitated and their bodies floated across the bay on mock crucifixes.
The bodies of the knights were decapitated and their bodies floated across the bay on mock crucifixes.

claims.claim: In response to the floating bodies, Grand Master de Valette beheaded his Turkish prisoners and fired their heads from cannons.

evidence.quote: In response, de Valette beheaded all his Turkish prisoners, loaded their heads into his cannons, and fired them into the Turkish camp.
De Valette answered by firing the heads of Turkish prisoners from cannons into the Ottoman camp.

claims.claim: An Ottoman waterborne attack on Senglea was devastated by a shore-level gun battery at the base of Fort St. Angelo, which killed or drowned around 800 attackers.

evidence.quote: battery of five cannons that had been constructed by Commander Chevalier de Guiral at the base of Fort St. Angelo with the sole purpose of stopping such an amphibious attack. Just two salvos sank all but one of the vessels, killing or drowning over 800 of the attackers.
sea-and-land assault was thrown back when guns from Fort St Angelo hit dozens of Ottoman boats in the harbour, killing or drowning around 800 men.

claims.claim: On August 7, a major Turkish assault on Fort St. Michael and Birgu was called off because a small Christian force from Mdina raided the unprotected Turkish camp.

evidence.quote: cavalry commander Captain Vincenzo Anastagi, on his daily sortie from Mdina, had attacked the unprotected Turkish field hospital, killing everyone and beheading more than sixty Turks. The Turks, thinking the Christian relief had arrived from Sicily, broke off their assault.
A small group of Hospitallers had ridden out of the city and launched a daring raid on the unguarded Ottoman camp, burning tents and slaughtering the sick and wounded.

claims.claim: On September 7, a relief force of about 8,000 men landed on Malta to assist the defenders.

evidence.quote: On 7 September, García de Toledo had, at last, landed 8,000 men at St. Paul's Bay on the north end of the island.
On 7 September, roughly 8,000 Sicilian reinforcements under Don Garcia de Toledo

claims.claim: By September 8, the demoralized Ottomans began withdrawing and preparing to leave the island.

evidence.quote: By 8 September, the Turks had embarked their artillery and were preparing to leave the island
The demoralised Ottomans began pulling out on 8 September, abandoning artillery

claims.claim: At the Battle of Djerba in May 1560, the Ottoman fleet surprised a Christian fleet and captured or sank about half its ships.

evidence.quote: Battle of Djerba in May 1560, when Ottoman admiral Piyale Pasha surprised the Christian fleet off the Tunisian island of Djerba, capturing or sinking about half the Christian ships.
battle of Djerba in May 1560, when Ottoman admiral Piyale Pasha surprised the Christian fleet off the Tunisian island of Djerba, capturing or sinking about half the enemy ships.

claims.claim: In mid-1564, the notorious seafarer Romegas captured several large merchantmen, including one belonging to the Chief Eunuch of the seraglio, taking high-ranking prisoners.

evidence.quote: In mid-1564, Romegas, the Order's most notorious seafarer, captured several large merchantmen, including one that belonged to the Chief Eunuch of the seraglio, and took numerous high-ranking prisoners

In mid 1564, Romegas, the Order's most notorious seafarer, captured several large merchantmen, including one that belonged to the Chief Eunuch of the Seraglio, and took numerous high-ranking prisoners

claims.claim: Jean Parisot de Valette was elected Grand Master of the Knights of Malta in 1557.

evidence.quote: In 1557, the Knights elected Jean Parisot de Valette Grand Master of the Order.
In 1557, Jean Parisot de Valette was elected Grand Master of the Order.

claims.claim: In 1551, the corsair Dragut and Sinan invaded Gozo and took virtually the entire population of approximately 5,000 people into captivity.

evidence.quote: sacked the town and took virtually the entire population of Gozo (approximately 5000 people) into captivity.
Taking virtually the entire population of Gozo (approximately 5,000 people) into captivity,

disputed: The exact size of the Ottoman army (Balbi di Correggio lists 48,000 invaders, whereas contemporary letters and Turkish registers suggest a lower count of 23,000 to 30,000; the script should present these varying estimates).

The exact cause of Dragut's death (one account claims he was killed by stone splinters from a cannonball fired too low by his own gunners, while Bosio claims it was a lucky shot from Fort St. Angelo; the script should state it was from a stray shot or artillery fire and attribute the accounts).

The August 20 climax involving a mine explosion and de Valette's counter-charge (Bradford describes a mine exploding and de Valette leading a desperate charge, but Balbi merely states de Valette ran to a threatened post, and Bosio mentions no mine detonation but rather a friendly fire panic; the script should focus on de Valette's personal leadership at the walls rather than a specific mine explosion).
